note: REASONING, MADE CHECKABLE. The work verifier checks output and cannot check reasoning — it can tell whether a figure carries a date, not whether a conclusion was sound. This closes that, not by inspecting the thinking but by recording what the thinking PREDICTED and checking later whether it held.
law: Every consequential decision records: what was chosen, what was REJECTED and why, and the falsifiable prediction it implies. A decision with no prediction cannot be graded, and an ungradable decision teaches nothing — it is an opinion with a timestamp.
whyThisWorks: You cannot audit a chain of thought after the fact; the reasoner will reconstruct a tidier version than the one they had. But a prediction made in advance is fixed, and reality grades it without argument. Over a hundred decisions this produces something no amount of introspection could: a measured hit rate per KIND of decision, which says where the judgment is reliable and where it is not.
costNote: Roughly 500 bytes each. Ten thousand decisions is about 1 MB in git against a 77 MB repo. Space is not a consideration and should never be the reason to record less.

grades.FAILED: it did not, and the decision was wrong
grades.UNTESTABLE: the prediction turned out not to be checkable — a fault in how it was written, and worth recording as such

decisions.decision: Retire the eBay-vs-TCGplayer Spread from headline selection, keeping it as a labelled stat.
decisions.rejected: Keep it with a permanent caveat on every appearance.
decisions.reasoning: The bias is permanent and unmeasurable — our eBay figure includes shipping, TCGplayer's never does, and no source at any tier closes it. A number needing a caveat every time it appears is doing more explaining than working.
decisions.predicts: No instrument built on the Spread will be missed. If within 60 days we find ourselves wanting it back for a real question, the retirement was wrong.

decisions.decision: Refresh the whole universe daily while it fits the budget; tier only as a fallback.
decisions.rejected: Tier by value from the start, accepting up to 90-day staleness on bulk.
decisions.reasoning: 16,675 items against a 20,000 allowance is 83%. Staleness we do not have to accept is staleness we should not accept.
decisions.predicts: Daily refresh of everything will stay inside budget until the universe exceeds ~18,000 items. If we breach the allowance before then, the arithmetic was wrong.

decisions.decision: Withdraw every graded price until the provider exposes a date range on sold aggregates.
decisions.rejected: Keep publishing them with a 'historical average' label.
decisions.reasoning: A label does not make a windowless median comparable to a current raw price. The subtraction itself is invalid, not just the presentation — and this one nearly reached a reader.
decisions.predicts: No graded claim will be publishable until a windowed source exists. If we find a defensible way to publish one WITHOUT a window, the withdrawal was over-cautious.
decisions.decidedBy: chat, after Tyler caught the error

decisions.decision: Agents advise and never block; only guards block, plus security as the single exception.
decisions.rejected: Let high-severity agent findings fail the run.
decisions.reasoning: An agent that can halt the pipeline turns a false positive into an outage. Every failure an agent finds is recoverable; a leaked credential is not.
decisions.predicts: No agent false-positive will ever cost us a publication day. If a run is lost to an agent's mistake, the exception list is wrong.

decisions.decision: Treat the Charizard/Blastoise post as the specification for art content: same artist, both hero cards, a gap long enough to surprise, household Pokemon.
decisions.rejected: Keep generating art posts by recency or by whatever the data made easy.
decisions.reasoning: One post landed after five failed. The difference was that both cards were wanted and the gap was long enough to be a story. Recency produced a common card and an underwhelming post.
decisions.predicts: The next three art posts built to this spec will each get more engagement than the Keldeo-style recency pick would have. If a recency pick outperforms a spec pick, the model is wrong.

decisions.decision: The creator portal offers angles and editable seeds, never finished tweets.
decisions.rejected: Ship ready-to-post copy so a creator can publish in one click.
decisions.reasoning: One-click copy would be used verbatim by most, and identical text across accounts destroys the credibility of every account using it, including ours.
decisions.predicts: Creators using the portal will post visibly different wording from each other. If we see two accounts publish the same sentence, the seeds are too finished and need to be shortened to fragments.
decisions.decidedBy: chat, correcting its own earlier over-rigid stance

decisions.decision: The watermark IS the free tier. Everything is free and watermarked; removing it becomes a gated feature later.
decisions.rejected: Gate the tool itself, or gate resolution, or gate how many composites somebody can make.
decisions.reasoning: Gating the TOOL stops the marketing before it starts - a creator who cannot make one never makes fifty. Gating resolution ships a worse product, which contradicts the whole standard. The watermark costs the user nothing they care about while free, and is the one thing a professional will pay to remove. It also means the free tier markets us on every post it makes, so the more it is used the more it is worth.
decisions.predicts: Creators will use the watermarked version freely and without complaint. If we see people cropping the mark out rather than asking to remove it, the mark is either too prominent or the value is not there yet.

decisions.decision: Blind packs of guards ship with published odds and a guaranteed tangible good. No buy-back, no cash-out.
decisions.rejected: A sell-back path for instant liquidity on a rare pull.
decisions.reasoning: The cash-out was the single element that turned a blind box into something regulators legislate. Without it this is the Funko/LEGO/Sonny Angel structure, which is on every toy-shop shelf. Removing it costs one feature and removes the entire category of problem.
decisions.predicts: Demand for packs will not depend on liquidity. If people ask for a sell-back path within 90 days of launch, the collectible framing is not carrying it on its own and the product needs rethinking rather than a buy-back bolted on.

decisions.decision: The tools are free permanently. Monetisation is physical product — guards — sold into the community the tools build. The landing page says CLOSED BETA and FREE FOREVER, in public.
decisions.rejected: Calling it a trial, which implies the free period ends; and any tools-based subscription or paywalled tier.
decisions.reasoning: Trial tells somebody the free thing ends and they will be asked for money later. Beta tells them they are early to something that stays. That is not a softer word, it is a truer one — charging for the tools is a business we are not running, and calling it a trial would set an expectation we would then have to break. Build a loyal base with free tools, sell real objects into it.
decisions.predicts: Nobody asks what it will cost. If waitlist replies contain pricing questions, the FREE FOREVER line is not landing and the page needs to say it louder rather than differently.

decisions.decision: A post QUEUE, not a posting agent. Tyler writes in batches, the machine sends at a set hour. It will not generate post text, will not post to anybody else's account, and will not send anything Tyler has not read.
decisions.rejected: An agent that writes and posts autonomously; and posting on other people's accounts.
decisions.reasoning: Our own outcome log: every post that worked was written by Tyler from his mood in the moment, and ZERO of them used any of the 84 formulas we generate. An agent that writes is automating the only part that works; an agent that presses send is automating the part that does not. Tyler named the bottleneck himself — being at the keyboard at 9pm, not thinking of something to say. Cost is not the constraint: pay-per-use is /bin/sh.015 a post, about ninety cents a month at two a day.
decisions.predicts: Queued posts perform in the same range as live ones. If they underperform consistently, the thing that mattered was posting in the moment rather than the words, and the queue should be scrapped rather than improved.

decisions.decision: FREE FOREVER covers the tools: binder pages, post images, streaks, want lists, the data. Posting on somebody's behalf is a paid service, because it costs $0.015-$0.20 of real money EVERY TIME it runs.
decisions.rejected: Leaving the line unstated and hoping nobody notices; and paywalling any tool that is currently free.
decisions.reasoning: The tools cost us nothing to run — they are static, so free forever is easy to keep because there is no marginal cost. Posting has a per-use cost that scales with volume, so charging for it is PASSING THROUGH A COST rather than paywalling a free thing. But that is only defensible if we say it plainly in that language: somebody who joined for FREE FOREVER and then finds the useful automation is paid will read it as bait and switch unless the distinction was stated before they signed up.
decisions.predicts: No waitlist reply accuses us of bait and switch when posting launches paid. If any does, the line was not stated clearly enough and the page needs to carry it.

decisions.decision: Line suggestions are ORDERED by follower count, not filtered. Under 1k prefers observation and confession and lowers questions; 5k-25k is where the permission mechanic is documented working; 25k+ can carry a divisive question. Every threshold is labelled unproven on screen.
decisions.rejected: Hiding registers outright, and presenting the thresholds as findings.
decisions.reasoning: Tyler found an asymmetry I missed: a question is a REQUEST, and an unanswered request is VISIBLY unanswered — a zero beside the reply icon — while an image is not a request and silence is not visible failure. So the shapes have different DOWNSIDES, not merely different upsides. I had been recommending questions off accounts at 16k-44k followers where there is always a crowd, and never checked whether the mechanic survives at low reach. tall_alan took ~900 replies at 16k; the same question at 500 followers takes three and looks worse than posting nothing. Ordering rather than hiding, because removing options would be the tool deciding for somebody and this account works because Tyler chooses the line.
decisions.predicts: Question-shaped posts underperform observation-shaped ones below roughly 1,000 followers. If the outcome log shows no difference once it holds twenty posts, the tiers are noise and should be deleted rather than tuned.

decisions.decision: Build for the Original Content Rewards originality standard rather than for raw reach. Every queued post must state, in writing and in advance, what is original about it, citing a field in our own catalogue — and a post with no stored claim does not ship, however well it would perform.
decisions.rejected: Optimising for what the outcome log rewards, which is views. The single-card art crop is cheap to make, fast to post, and our 127,200-view post is exactly the pattern the programme names as insufficient: third-party art, a watermark, and a text overlay describing what is visible. Reach and eligibility are not the same axis, and we were only measuring one of them.
decisions.reasoning: The programme pays for primary work and excludes reuploads, watermarks and basic descriptive overlays. Our best-performing format sits on that line, and the deciding reading belongs to a reviewer we never meet. Given that, the cheap protection is not producing safer posts — it is being able to show, per post, dated and written beforehand, what the original contribution was and which of our own data produced it. Writing that sentence is also the check: 'we cropped a card' is very hard to type into a field labelled 'what is original here', and noticing you cannot answer is the whole mechanism.
decisions.predicts: Analysis-led posts — the ones where a fact from our catalogue is the post — will pass the originality guard, and single-card art crops will not. Concretely: of the five logged posts, the Arita illustrator pairing and the Slakoth printed-attack-name post can each cite a catalogue field and state a contribution that is not a restatement of the caption; the Charmander mood crop cannot, and the Mabosstiff pun cannot cite anything in our data because nothing in this repo describes what is DRAWN on a card. If, after twenty posts, art crops turn out to pass the guard as readily as analysis-led ones, then the guard is checking prose quality rather than originality and should be deleted rather than tuned.

decisions.decision: Ship every catalogue card in the editor index (16,468 rows) rather than the post-worthy subset (6,725), with the tail carrying only the columns search and display need. Findability is the product: Tyler could not find the card he wanted because it was never in the page, and both Magmar cards from the 2026-08-25 post were absent.
decisions.rejected: Keeping the hero-only filter. It made the editor work but made it unable to answer the question people actually bring to it, and no amount of query-parser work fixes an index that does not contain the card.
decisions.cost: build.html goes from 2.00MB to 2.83MB of inline script. The filter it replaces was introduced in c6ed73e on 2026-08-24 as a MOBILE CRASH FIX, not a page-weight preference: at 4.49MB the inline script killed mobile Safari and Chrome, taking photos, moods and angles with it, and the fix brought the page to 2.14MB. This change spends roughly a third of the headroom that fix bought back.
decisions.mistakeToRecord: I removed that filter on a page-weight argument, having measured only the GZIP transfer delta (+201KB). Gzip size is not what broke mobile Safari - parsed inline script size is, and I did not check why the filter existed before removing it. The measurement answered a question nobody was asking. The commit message that introduced the filter said plainly what it was for and I did not read it until asked.
decisions.risk: UNVERIFIED ON DEVICE. No phone has run the current page. The failure this risks is the one already in the error ledger as error 32, on the device class where X traffic overwhelmingly is, and on the same device whose canvas memory limits produced the blank-export defect fixed earlier today. 2.83MB sits between the 2.14MB that is known to work and the 4.49MB that is known to fail, and nothing in this repo can tell us which side of the line it falls on.
decisions.whatWouldChangeIt: A real phone loading research/assets/build.html and searching for a Common. If the editor renders, the moods and angles appear and a search for 'magmar kimura' returns cards, the decision holds. If any of those is missing, the tail must move out of the inline script and be fetched on demand instead, which keeps findability and returns the page to roughly 2.0MB.
decisions.checkWith: Tyler, on his own phone. This cannot be checked from here.
decisions.status: PROVISIONAL - shipped, unverified on the device it risks
decisions.predicts: The editor loads on Tyler's phone at 3.00MB of inline script, renders its photos, moods and angles, and a search for a Common returns cards. If any of those fails, the tail moves out of the inline script and is fetched on demand, which keeps findability and returns the page to roughly 2.0MB.

decisions.decision: Three tiers of promise, stated separately so none of them can be read as another. (1) The FREE TIER stays free — no expiry, no card, no bait. (2) SOME FEATURES BECOME PAID LATER; which ones is not decided here, only that the possibility is disclosed before anyone signs up rather than after. (3) EARLY WAITLIST TESTERS WHO REPORT DURING THE BETA KEEP THE FULL TOOLSET FREE PERMANENTLY — everything, including whatever later goes paid.
decisions.reasoning: THE CONDITION IS EARNED ONCE, NOT ONGOING. Report during the beta and free-for-life is yours unconditionally from that moment. An ongoing condition — stay helpful or lose it — creates low-grade anxiety about how much is enough and what happens if you go quiet, and people respond by over-reporting to stay safe or by disengaging quietly. Both destroy the only thing the arrangement exists to buy, which is honest feedback. A tester who says 'this is worse than what I already use' must have nothing to lose by saying it.
decisions.rejected: An ongoing contribution requirement, and a points or tier scheme. Fifteen people do not need a loyalty programme, and the moment the reward is metered the feedback optimises for the meter.
decisions.cost: A permanent liability of unknown size against a paid tier that does not exist yet. It is small and bounded — the beta cohort is roughly fifteen — and it is the cheapest honest price for feedback from people who have no reason to flatter us.
decisions.mistakeToRecord: THE PUBLIC CLAIM IS ALREADY BROADER THAN THIS POLICY. research/assets/index-landing.html says 'Free forever · early access before anyone else' and 'Free.' with no scope attached, and decision 2026-08-23-tools-free-forever records the landing page saying FREE FOREVER in public. A stranger reads that as everything, forever, and it attaches on THEIR reading rather than ours. This decision narrows an unscoped promise that is already live, which is the wrong order to do it in.
supersedes: 2026-08-23-tools-free-forever — kept in spirit, narrowed in scope: 'the tools are free permanently' becomes 'the free tier stays free', because 'the tools' had no boundary and every feature we build enlarges it.

2026-08-24-what-free-forever-covers — consistent with this and more specific. It already carved posting-on-your-behalf out as paid on a pass-through-cost basis. This generalises that carve-out and says so BEFORE signup rather than at the point somebody hits the wall.
decisions.risk: Somebody who joined under the unscoped 'Free forever' line reads the narrower terms as a walk-back. That reading is available to them and it is not unreasonable, which is why the terms must reach existing waitlist members directly rather than only appearing on the page for new arrivals.
decisions.openQuestion: WE CANNOT TELL WHO REPORTED. The honesty box is anonymous by construction and that must not change — the whole reason it produces usable answers is that nothing identifies the sender. So qualification cannot be derived from it. Three candidates queued to Tyler as editor-61: the questionnaire's optional name field, an explicit opt-in on the form, or Tyler's own judgement of who actually helped. His call, not ours.
decisions.whatWouldChangeIt: Tyler decides the paid tier never happens, in which case tiers (2) and (3) collapse into (1) and the terms get simpler. Or the beta cohort grows past roughly fifty, at which point 'Tyler's judgement' stops being a workable qualification rule and needs a recorded opt-in.
decisions.checkWith: Read the four-sentence draft in research/beta-terms-draft.md and say whether it is what he meant. Nothing ships until he does.
decisions.predicts: If the terms are right, nobody in the beta asks a follow-up question about what happens to their access. A single 'so what happens after the beta?' reply means the four sentences did not do their job and need to be plainer, not longer.
decisions.buildsNothing: No accounts, no billing, no entitlement flags, deliberately. Fifteen people do not need infrastructure, and building an entitlement system now would commit us to a shape for the paid tier before we know what it is.

decisions.decision: verify-work and pre-mortem stay BLOCKING for shipping the editor and any user-facing artifact, and become ADVISORY inside scheduled data jobs. They report in full either way; only their power to stop the run changes, and only where the run's product is data rather than something a person will look at.
decisions.reasoning: Tyler, 2026-08-26: 'A ledger about our work quality should not stop prices from publishing.' The distinction is WHAT THE FINDING IS ABOUT. 'Six guards not yet interrogated' and '24 facts rest only on secondary sources' are true, worth fixing, and carry no information about whether tonight's eBay medians are right. Letting them gate a data publication means the freshness of public prices depends on whether somebody has finished a code-review chore — two entirely unrelated things wired together by nothing more than both living in generate-pulse.
decisions.rejected: Downgrading them everywhere, which would waste guards Tyler asked for by name. And leaving them blocking everywhere, which is what produced six days of stale public prices behind a citation backlog.
decisions.cost: A scheduled run can now go green while carrying real work-quality findings. Mitigated because both still print in full, both still block the fleet run Tyler actually reads, and artifact-freshness is blocking so a data job that produces nothing still fails.
decisions.mistakeToRecord: I wired both into generate-pulse as bare imports without asking what their findings were ABOUT. A guard's blast radius is part of its design and I treated it as an implementation detail — the same error as letting an advisory guard set process.exitCode.
decisions.risk: A finding that genuinely should stop a data publication gets classified here by habit. The guard against that is the narrowness: this covers exactly two scripts, both of which check US rather than the artifact, and every guard that checks the artifact itself stays bare and blocking.
decisions.whatWouldChangeIt: Either of them growing a check about the DATA rather than about our process. At that point the check belongs in a data guard, not in a widened exemption here.
decisions.checkWith: Whether a scheduled run ever goes green while something he would have wanted stopped slipped through.
decisions.predicts: Scheduled data jobs stop failing on process debt, and nothing user-facing ships with an un-interrogated guard, because the fleet run still refuses it.

decisions.decision: card-guard checks the cards THIS RUN produced — today's dated files plus the latest-* aliases the pipeline rewrites every run — rather than all 105 svg files ever committed. A --all flag re-reads everything for a deliberate audit.
decisions.reasoning: Tyler, 2026-08-26: 'The protection stays, the job can go green, and we do not hand-edit history to satisfy a guard.' It was failing the daily job on a dash rendered in 2026-08-21-social.svg, -22 and -23 — cards published days ago that nobody will re-render. A guard that can only be satisfied by editing history can never go green, and one that can never go green gets skimmed, which is how it stops working at all. This repo has logged the same shape once already: run-tests asserted card artifacts no pipeline produced, so it was checking committed fossils, and deleting one killed the whole daily run.
decisions.rejected: Hand-editing the three historical cards. It would have turned the guard green while teaching us that the way to satisfy a guard is to rewrite the past.
decisions.cost: A defect introduced into an old card and never re-minted is no longer caught by the scheduled run. --all exists for that, and the cards it would miss are ones nothing regenerates.
decisions.mistakeToRecord: The scoping immediately proved its own worth in the other direction: with the fossils gone, the one card-level finding left was REAL — latest-social.svg rendered 'per pack' as an em dash whenever the figure was missing, on a card whose whole purpose is measured values. It had been sitting behind the noise of three fossils. Fixed by omitting the tile rather than dashing it, which is card-guard's own rule: either the value exists or the slot should not.
decisions.risk: Somebody reads the smaller number of checked cards as weaker coverage rather than as correctly aimed coverage.
decisions.whatWouldChangeIt: Historical cards becoming re-publishable, at which point they are current output again and in scope.
decisions.checkWith: card-guard --all, run when a card is re-minted from history.
decisions.predicts: Card-level findings on the daily run drop to near zero and the ones that appear are about cards minted that morning.
